questions.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =0,$
then what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =0.$ So, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 6{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 & 0 \\ 6 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 

From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{2}{3}.$

questions.problem:
Given that $\lambda =-5$ and $\lambda =8$ are the eigenvalues of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ 6 & 7\end{aligned}]$,
find two linearly independent eigenvectors of $A.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each of the eigenvalues separately. 

- For $\lambda =-5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ 6 & 7\end{aligned}]-(-5)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 6 & 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 6{x}_{1}+12{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 6 & 12 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-6){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 
From the first equation, we obtain  ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For $\lambda =8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ 6 & 7\end{aligned}]-8[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-12 & 2 \\ 6 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-12{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 6{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-12 & 2 & 0 \\ 6 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-12 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 
From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{6}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=6,$ we get the eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 6\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, two linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix $A$ are

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 6\end{aligned}].
$$

that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\,\lambda=2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =2.$ So, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -4 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 & 0 \\ 5 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). So, $x_2$ is a free variable. 

From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
5x_1-4x_2=0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x_1=\dfrac{4}{5}x_2.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating an Eigenvector Corresponding to an Eigenvalue

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding Two Linearly Independent Eigenvectors of a 2x2 Matrix
canonical_examples.problem:
Given that $\lambda=1$ and $\lambda=-4$ are the eigenvalues of the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130716/assets/b1b6bc95f7d29e0c64007e7c19a4690eb3def3e58d677d8a21604315bbb21c0a.svg)
find two linearly independent eigenvectors of $A.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can get two linearly independent eigenvectors by simply finding eigenvectors corresponding to the different eigenvalues.

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each of the eigenvalues separately. 

- For $\lambda =1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]-1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We have to solve the corresponding system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $2$nd one). So, $x_1$ is a free variable. 
From the first equation, we obtain  $x_2=0.$ Therefore, the general solution is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130716/assets/812c2f9dfcb3943cc13c47d2f1b85d9b1a67ce10c9e6a965a9bb915655d0316c.svg)
Setting, for instance, $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130716/assets/7d3a9e02893b98a2739398d48138be4c930ea87b3e3577776cfdd7edf6faf4e7.svg)

- For $\lambda =-4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]-(-4)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We have to solve the corresponding system of linear equations:

$$

Consider the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130716/assets/30880937eed54b00cb0ebe13bd2a46e2634e4193343b1db552b30836ed1e055b.svg) Given that $\lambda=3$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ how can we find an eigenvector that corresponds to this eigenvalue?

Recall that a non-zero vector $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ with corresponding eigenvalue $\lambda$ if 

$$
A{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}}={\color{red}\lambda}{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}}.
$$

We can rewrite this equation, substituting ${\color{red}{\lambda = 3}},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =3v \\ Av-3v & =0 \\ Av-3Iv & =0 \\ (A-3I)v & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, to find an eigenvector of $A$ that corresponds to $\lambda = {\color{red}3},$ we need to find a non-zero solution of the equation 

$$
(A- {\color{red}3} I){\color{blue}\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{0}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 6 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 6 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation $(A- {\color{red}3} I){\color{blue}\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{0}$ corresponds to the following homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=0 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $A-{\color{red}3}I$ is already in row echelon form, and it has one pivot column (the $1$st one). So, $x_2$ is a free variable. Moreover, from the first equation, we get $x_1=6x_2,$ which implies that the general solution is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130716/assets/fa0625bc99de3a27874b5695e72c9fd2e41ab618e49228086df7efcf7e1bb04f.svg)

We only require one eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda={\color{red}3}.$ Setting $x_2=1,$ we obtain the eigenvector

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130716/assets/bcd87529387e7c400b7f5ccd896cfcbe3e42ab386a5b9d84b565f12752e2c4c3.svg) 

**Note:** If we set $x_2=2,$ we'll get a different eigenvector, namely
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130716/assets/83541fd42d19f0e3b17be1c36983d50d1382f36352168bce2d148126db7bf265.svg)
Note that $\mathbf w$ is also an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda=3.$ In fact, we can choose any real $x_2 \neq 0$ to generate an eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda = 3.$ 

**Watch out!** In the case of $x_2=0,$ we get the zero vector, but this is not an eigenvector. Remember that eigenvectors must be non-zero vectors.

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
Consider the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130716/assets/30880937eed54b00cb0ebe13bd2a46e2634e4193343b1db552b30836ed1e055b.svg) Given that $\lambda=3$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ how can we find an eigenvector that corresponds to this eigenvalue?

Recall that a non-zero vector $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ with corresponding eigenvalue $\lambda$ if 

$$
A{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}}={\color{red}\lambda}{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}}.
$$

We can rewrite this equation, substituting ${\color{red}{\lambda = 3}},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =3v \\ Av-3v & =0 \\ Av-3Iv & =0 \\ (A-3I)v & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, to find an eigenvector of $A$ that corresponds to $\lambda = {\color{red}3},$ we need to find a non-zero solution of the equation 

$$
(A- {\color{red}3} I){\color{blue}\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{0}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 6 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 6 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation $(A- {\color{red}3} I){\color{blue}\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{0}$ corresponds to the following homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=0 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $A-{\color{red}3}I$ is already in row echelon form, and it has one pivot column (the $1$st one). So, $x_2$ is a free variable. Moreover, from the first equation, we get $x_1=6x_2,$ which implies that the general solution is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130716/assets/fa0625bc99de3a27874b5695e72c9fd2e41ab618e49228086df7efcf7e1bb04f.svg)

We only require one eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda={\color{red}3}.$ Setting $x_2=1,$ we obtain the eigenvector

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130716/assets/bcd87529387e7c400b7f5ccd896cfcbe3e42ab386a5b9d84b565f12752e2c4c3.svg) 

**Note:** If we set $x_2=2,$ we'll get a different eigenvector, namely
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130716/assets/83541fd42d19f0e3b17be1c36983d50d1382f36352168bce2d148126db7bf265.svg)
Note that $\mathbf w$ is also an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda=3.$ In fact, we can choose any real $x_2 \neq 0$ to generate an eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda = 3.$ 

**Watch out!** In the case of $x_2=0,$ we get the zero vector, but this is not an eigenvector. Remember that eigenvectors must be non-zero vectors.

tutorials.name: Connection Between Eigenspaces and Null Spaces
tutorials.problem:
Given a matrix $A$ with an eigenvalue $\lambda$, the **eigenspace** $V_\lambda$ can be defined as the set of all possible eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda$ plus the vector $\mathbf{0}{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130716/assets/78c2c84d57ef00f32675c6d56fa91af39e0680eadf05ec266b0bdab9a57a8388.svg)

Note that the eigenspace consists of *all* (not only non-zero) solutions of the equation $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.$ So, the eigenspace can also be viewed as the *null space* of the matrix $A-\lambda I,$ as follows:

$$
V_{\color{red}\lambda} = \textrm{Null}(A - {\color{red}\lambda} I).
$$

We also have the following theorem:

*Eigenvectors that correspond to different eigenvalues are always linearly independent.*

For example, the matrix 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130716/assets/e3c63b7efcb927079757e6f0e3e008a6f5038e11957524f51e1b1f45fdecd5f7.svg)

has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=-2$ and $\lambda_2=-1,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130716/assets/1c5df8239dae6efdd15a27498a9535b855004e3570c8eff46534993b9ec1e75f.svg)

tutorials.title: Connection Between Eigenspaces and Null Spaces
tutorials.content:
Given a matrix $A$ with an eigenvalue $\lambda$, the **eigenspace** $V_\lambda$ can be defined as the set of all possible eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda$ plus the vector $\mathbf{0}{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130716/assets/78c2c84d57ef00f32675c6d56fa91af39e0680eadf05ec266b0bdab9a57a8388.svg)

Note that the eigenspace consists of *all* (not only non-zero) solutions of the equation $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.$ So, the eigenspace can also be viewed as the *null space* of the matrix $A-\lambda I,$ as follows:

$$
V_{\color{red}\lambda} = \textrm{Null}(A - {\color{red}\lambda} I).
$$

We also have the following theorem:

*Eigenvectors that correspond to different eigenvalues are always linearly independent.*

For example, the matrix 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130716/assets/e3c63b7efcb927079757e6f0e3e008a6f5038e11957524f51e1b1f45fdecd5f7.svg)

has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=-2$ and $\lambda_2=-1,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130716/assets/1c5df8239dae6efdd15a27498a9535b855004e3570c8eff46534993b9ec1e75f.svg) 

Here, $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ are linearly independent (they are not collinear).

**Watch out!** Eigenvectors that correspond to the *same* eigenvalue *can be* (and very often *will* be) linearly dependent. For example, the vectors

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130716/assets/c303fb73d6fc039bfa536d6f7de3103e774d913d2514c10c17d59fcf48d5bf00.svg)

are collinear eigenvectors of the matrix $A$ above that correspond to $\lambda_2=-1.$
